arbiters.name: NASA JPL Horizons (DE441) apparent geocentric ecliptic positions, carried into the IAU 2006/2000A true ecliptic and equinox of date
arbiters.source: NASA JPL Horizons API 1.2 (https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api), fetched 2026-09-22: ephemeris DE441 for every target, with Mars to Pluto as their system barycentres (NAIF 4 to 9); EOP file eop.260922.p261219 (data 1962-01-20 to 2026-09-22, predictions to 2026-12-18). One request per target: EPHEM_TYPE OBSERVER, CENTER 500@399 (the geocentre), QUANTITIES 31 (observer ecliptic longitude and latitude of date of the apparent position: light-time, gravitational deflection by the Sun, stellar aberration), APPARENT AIRLESS, TIME_TYPE TT, TLIST_TYPE JD with the 24 jd_tt values to 8 decimals, ANG_FORMAT DEG, EXTRA_PREC YES, CSV_FORMAT YES. The responses are kept verbatim in sources/horizons-24/, byte for byte as committed in the zodiacs.org site repository (ZodiacsOfficial/site, docs/platform/evidence/engine-beyond-swiss/corpora/horizons-24/, commit 3f31ba17), together with Horizons's body-centre files for Mars to Pluto (NAIF 499 to 999, from the satellite solutions mar099, jup365_merged, sat441l, ura184_merged, nep098_merged, plu060_merged), fetched the same way and used only for the body-centre measurement in the uncertainty. Plus the frame conversion: Horizons labels this frame IAU76/80 ecliptic-of-date, and the eopJpl model of it, with its per-instant celestial-pole offsets, is the horizons-frame study in the same repository (docs/platform/evidence/engine-beyond-swiss/horizons-frame/: decompose.py, results.json), the offsets copied into sources/horizons-24/frame-offsets.json.
arbiters.uncertainty: Frame model: the eopJpl model of Horizons's frame was first identified in the horizons-frame study, which compared four candidate models (bare, bias, eopJpl, eopIers) against Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03's IAU 2006/2000A positions for these same 240 Horizons directions; there eopJpl left at most 5.45 mas in longitude (median 1.40 mas) and 1.86 mas in latitude (results.json summary.eopJpl). In this suite the model's acceptance rests on validate.py's independent reduction from DE440s, not on Swiss: for the nine bodies other than the Moon it differs from the expected values by at most 2.82 mas in longitude and 0.22 mas in latitude, and at each instant their longitude differences agree to within 0.37 mas, so what the model leaves is a rotation common to all bodies. Print precision: Horizons prints 1e-7 deg (0.36 mas), so each angle it gives carries up to 0.18 mas of rounding; the 0.001 mas rounding of the recorded offsets is negligible. Barycentres: Mars to Pluto are the planets' system barycentres from DE441 (NAIF 4 to 9), as every other target is DE441's. A planet's body centre differs from its barycentre by what its satellites do to it. Measured here as Horizons's body-centre files minus its barycentre files, both converted as above, that is at most (longitude/latitude, arcsec) Mars 0.0000/0.0000, Jupiter 0.0583/0.0029, Saturn 0.0414/0.0230, Pluto 0.0752/0.0835 over these 24 instants, varying from instant to instant as the satellites move; for Uranus and Neptune the satellites' pull is at most about 45 km and 74 km, under 4 mas from the Earth. So an engine that returns body centres consistent with DE441 instead of barycentres differs from these vectors by no more than 0.0835 arcsec. Horizons's body-centre files for Uranus and Neptune, which come from the satellite solutions ura184_merged and nep098_merged, depart from DE441's barycentres by far more, up to 0.6714/0.0104 (Uranus) and 0.1087/0.0047 (Neptune); the departure drifts with time, from at most 0.0529 and 0.0094 arcsec between 1962 and 2026 to 0.6714 arcsec at 2148-12-30 and 0.1087 arcsec at 2125-02-11, and it is why the suite does not use them. DE440's barycentres agree with DE441's to within 3 mas (the check below). Independent check: an apparent-place reduction from DE440s (arbiters/l1/validate.py with jplephem and pyerfa: light-time iteration, deflection by the Sun, annual aberration, pnm06a and the true obliquity; kernel de440s.bsp, sha256 c1c7feeab882263fc493a9d5a5b2ddd71b54826cdf65d8d17a76126b260a49f2), with Mars to Pluto as the system barycentres 4 to 9 as in the vectors, differs from the 240 expected values by a median of 1.27 mas in longitude and at most 0.95 mas in latitude. For the nine bodies other than the Moon the longitude differences agree at each instant to within 0.37 mas, so what is left is a rotation common to all of them, the frame model's remainder, at most 2.82 mas (1969-07-20); the Moon differs by up to 12.63 mas (1851-03-14). Evaluating at the TLIST value Horizons was sent (jd_tt to 8 decimals of a day) instead of at jd_tt moves no position by more than 0.28 mas. Per-body statistics are in arbiters/l1/validation.json. The Moon's larger difference comes from the ephemerides, not the arbiter: once the common rotation is taken out it follows, instant by instant, the horizons-frame study's frame-free comparison of geometric positions (horizons-frame/vectors/results.json), which puts DE440s's Moon 10.24 mas from DE441's at 1851-03-14 and 8.60 mas at 2148-12-30.

arbiters.name: ERFA sidereal time and obliquity; spherical geometry of the angles
arbiters.source: ERFA 2.0.1 through pyerfa 2.0.1.5 (github.com/liberfa/erfa, derived from IAU SOFA): gst06a, obl06, nut06a. UT1−UTC: IERS finals2000A (the IERS Rapid Service/Prediction Centre finals.all fetched 2026-09-22, sha256 c672540e026d3cd4840c0858d4ce2bc4a18c3bc9751f9636c3285e11950d58a1; the three columns used are the committed CSV). TAI−UTC: IERS Bulletin C, hpiers.obspm.fr/iers/bul/bulc/Leap_Second.dat (through Bulletin C 72, fetched 2026-09-28). ΔT outside the IERS span: F. Espenak and J. Meeus, Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: −1999 to +3000, NASA/TP-2006-214141 (2006). Definitions: R. W. Holden, The Elements of House Division (1977); M. P. Munkasey, An Astrological House Formulary; W. M. Smart, Textbook on Spherical Astronomy.
arbiters.uncertainty: Numerical: each value is computed by two independent routes (great-circle intersections of unit vectors, and the classical closed forms) and checked against its defining property with ERFA coordinate routines (s2c, rx, c2s, hd2ae); over this arbiter's 70 vectors the largest disagreement is 4e-09″. Time: TT is pinned by input.jd_tt; moving ΔT by 60 s moves no output by more than 0.00048″ (median 9e-05″), because IAU 2006 sidereal time depends on TT only through precession-nutation (about 1e-4″ per minute) and the geometry amplifies that at most 9.1-fold. Model: the values are defined by IAU 2006/2000A; another sidereal-time or obliquity model moves them by the model difference times the amplification, here at most 4.0 (sidereal time) and 9.1 (obliquity) arcsec per arcsec (vectors at 10 or more carry a note). Recomputed through ERFA with IAU 2000B sidereal time and nutation they move by at most 0.043″; with IAU 1982/1994 sidereal time and the IAU 1980 obliquity and nutation by at most 1.2″, more than the tolerance on 2 of these vectors (each carries a note). Rounding: 1e-10°. An after-the-fact comparison with Swiss Ephemeris is reported in arbiters/l2/swiss-check.json (statistics only).

arbiters.name: Cusps that do not exist: the construction has no solution in zodiacal order
arbiters.source: Constructions: Placidus de Titis, Tabulae primi mobilis (Milan, 1657; English translation by J. Cooper, Primum Mobile, 1814); W. A. Koch and E. Schaeck, Häusertabellen des Geburtsortes (Göppingen, 1962); both restated in R. W. Holden, The Elements of House Division (L. N. Fowler, Romford, 1977; page numbers not verified for this file). TT, RAMC and ε as in l2-angles-erfa: ERFA 2.0.1 through pyerfa 2.0.1.5 (github.com/liberfa/erfa, derived from IAU SOFA): gst06a, obl06, nut06a. UT1−UTC: IERS finals2000A (the IERS Rapid Service/Prediction Centre finals.all fetched 2026-09-22, sha256 c672540e026d3cd4840c0858d4ce2bc4a18c3bc9751f9636c3285e11950d58a1; the three columns used are the committed CSV). TAI−UTC: IERS Bulletin C, hpiers.obspm.fr/iers/bul/bulc/Leap_Second.dat (through Bulletin C 72, fetched 2026-09-28). ΔT outside the IERS span: F. Espenak and J. Meeus, Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: −1999 to +3000, NASA/TP-2006-214141 (2006).
arbiters.uncertainty: None from the numbers: no failure is marginal. The Placidus residual moves by exactly the change of RAMC, so each Placidus failure survives any change of RAMC smaller than the largest closest miss of its unsolvable cusps, here at least 1.5°; each MC degree that never rises or sets has |tan φ tan δ_MC| ≥ 1.17; each order violation is at least 15.4°; and every failure was also verified at RAMC ± 0.1°. Model differences in sidereal time are of order 1 mas, legacy models 0.5″, so none can change a status.

arbiters.name: IANA tzdb 2025c with backzone, compiled by zic 2025c
arbiters.source: IANA time zone database release 2025c: https://data.iana.org/time-zones/releases/tzdata2025c.tar.gz (sha256 4aa79e4effee53fc4029ffe5f6ebe97937282ebcdf386d5d2da91ce84142f957) and https://data.iana.org/time-zones/releases/tzcode2025c.tar.gz (sha256 697ebe6625444aef5080f58e49d03424bbb52e08bf483d3ddb5acf10cbd15740), both OpenPGP-signed by Paul Eggert (key 7E37 92A9 D8AC F7D6 33BC 1588 ED97 E90E 62AA 7E34; signatures checked 2026-09-28). The data are the Makefile's `make PACKRATDATA=backzone PACKRATLIST=zone.tab` build: backzone's pre-1970 history for the zone.tab zones that the main data merge into links. Why backzone: a birth chart needs the local time in force where and when the birth happened, often before 1970, and tzdb's default build does not keep that history for these zones; it makes each of them a link to another zone whose clocks have agreed with it since 1970, so the zone answers with the other zone's history (Africa/Banjul at 1880-12-31T12:00:00 gets Abidjan's local mean time, -968 s, instead of its own, -3996 s). The maintainers' caveat applies: the Makefile of tzdata 2025c offers backzone as 'out-of-scope and often-wrong data', and its theory.html says the file 'is less reliable and does not necessarily follow database guidelines'. zic and zdump are built from the same release's tzcode.
arbiters.uncertainty: None in the computation: the three readers agree exactly on every vector. The data are tzdb's reconstruction, not history: offsets before 1970 are tzdb's best estimates and backzone's are the least reliable (see the maintainers' caveat under source), and some future offsets are predictions (the 2030 Ramadan rule, which tzdb 2026d has already replaced, and the 2035 summer time). A vector tests agreement with this build of tzdb 2025c.

arbiters.source: The definition of local mean time: mean solar time at east longitude lon runs ahead of UT by lon/15 hours, 240 s of UTC offset per degree.
arbiters.uncertainty: None: a definition. The 0.001 s tolerance only absorbs an implementation's floating-point rounding.

arbiters.name: IERS leap-second table (leap-seconds.list, tzdata 2025c)
arbiters.source: leap-seconds.list as distributed in tzdata 2025c (IERS Earth Orientation Centre, Paris Observatory; updated through IERS Bulletin C; last update 2025-07-07 (NTP 3960835200); expires 2026-06-28 (NTP 3991593600); its #h line, SHA-1 49db2447571e5e1b2f002a539c8da8e439b8e49e, verified). TT = TAI + 32.184 s exactly (IAU 1991 Resolution A4), so TT - UTC = 32.184 s + (TAI - UTC).
arbiters.uncertainty: None: TAI - UTC is an integer number of seconds by definition and 32.184 s is exact. The 0.5 ms tolerance only absorbs floating-point representation.

arbiters.name: IERS UT1 - UTC (finals2000A, observed rows) with the leap-second table
arbiters.source: UT1 - UTC per day at 0h UTC from the IERS finals.all (IAU 2000) file fetched 2026-09-22 (sha256 c672540e026d3cd4840c0858d4ce2bc4a18c3bc9751f9636c3285e11950d58a1, 3,767,520 bytes), extracted to CSV (MJD, date, I/P flag, UT1 - UTC, formal error) and copied here unchanged; TAI - UTC from leap-seconds.list of tzdata 2025c (arbiter iers-leap-seconds-2025c).
arbiters.uncertainty: The IERS formal error of UT1 - UTC on these rows is at most 0.0007116 s; the values are published to 0.1 microsecond, and TAI - UTC and 32.184 s are exact. The tolerance is 0.1 s: a Delta T error of 0.1 s moves the Moon by about 0.05 arcsec (its mean motion is about 0.55 arcsec per second of time), which keeps Delta T's share of the L1 positional tolerance (1 arcsec) near 5%.

arbiters.name: Julian and Gregorian calendar arithmetic, two published algorithms
arbiters.source: Richards, E. G. (2013), 'Calendars', in Urban & Seidelmann (eds.), Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac, 3rd ed., sec. 15.11 (Algorithms 3 and 4, Julian and Gregorian parameters); Fliegel, H. F. & Van Flandern, T. C. (1968), Communications of the ACM 11(10), 657; Meeus, J. (1998), Astronomical Algorithms, 2nd ed., ch. 7. Both calendars proleptic, astronomical year numbering; the JDN of a civil day is the Julian date at its noon.
arbiters.uncertainty: None: exact integer arithmetic, with independent published algorithms agreeing on every vector and on the dense range.

arbiters.uncertainty: Tolerances by kind: event.ingress: 2 s to 5250 s; event.lunation: 2 s to 3 s; event.station: 6270 s to 50406 s. Check (a): every solve repeated with half hour brackets agrees within 0.000 s, at most 0.0000 of its tolerance (limit 0.1). The array reduction agrees with validate.py's apparent() at every solved instant within 0.004172 mas. Property: at t - tolerance and t + tolerance every ingress lies on opposite sides of its target, at most 1.498 arcsec from it (limit 1.5). Vector L4-ING-0061 solves -0.0002 s from the independent de440.bsp reduction in docs/evidence/1.1.0-rc.11-20261115/breaker/results/ingress-ref.json (limit 1 s). Check (b), against the JPL Horizons API (version 1.2, ephemeris DE441, EOP file eop.261116.p270212), observer quantity 31 for the geocentre in TT, retrieved 2026-11-17 as recorded in sources/l4/horizons-provenance.tsv: 140 of 140 events checked, 0 failed and were dropped, 0 pending. For the 110 ingresses and lunations, Horizons' longitude at the solved instant differs from the target by a median of 0.047 arcsec; the worst is L4-ING-0049 (the first ingress of Neptune after 1860-01-01 TT) at -0.359 arcsec (limit 0.45). The difference grows with distance from J2000 (1860 to 1899: -0.359 to +0.011; 1900 to 1959: -0.158 to +0.002; 1960 to 2029: -0.057 to +0.003; 2030 to 2149: -0.012 to +0.343 arcsec), as the IAU 1976/1980 frame Horizons gives for quantity 31 parts from the IAU 2006/2000A frame of the arbiter. For the 30 stations, the station implied by Horizons' longitudes an hour either side of the solved instant lies at most 62 s from it; the largest share of a tolerance is L4-STA-0030 (the first station of Saturn after 2140-07-01 TT), +62 s against 49110 s (0.0013). runs.notes:
- **Positions (L1).** From 1.1.0-rc.9 a plain call computes on the sealed DE440 pack the package ships (`docs/de440.md`), and this run answers the 240 position requests with a plain `natalChart`, outside `withEphemeris`: nothing is opened by the adapter, nothing is supplied to it and nothing is fetched. All 240 pass. Against DE441 the largest differences are 0.0127″ in longitude and 0.0011″ in latitude, both the Moon's (L1-POS-0002 in 1851 and L1-POS-0222 in 2125); the other nine bodies are within 0.0038″ in longitude and 0.0003″ in latitude. The arbiter's own check against DE440s (`arbiters/l1/README.md`) puts the lunar difference between DE440 and DE441 at up to 12.63 mas in 1851. Mars to Pluto are system barycentres on both sides. Outside the pack's years (1790 to 2210), and after `setDefaultEphemeris("astronomy-engine")`, the engine computes on astronomy-engine: the next section runs it that way, and 48 of the 240 pass.
- **The pack.** SHA-256 `51428874d9a47213abc0ff42cbcec65f338624eaa2d8831f0e6ddc3654bf1fa7`, 2,489,664 bytes, refitted from NAIF's `de440.bsp` (SHA-256 `a4ce9bf9b3282becc9f4b2ac3cebe03a2ae7599981aabd7265fd8482fff7c4b5`) for 1790 to 2210. It is in the repository and in the package, so continuous integration reruns this section. The angles, houses and time vectors of this run come from the same plain calls; they do not depend on the ephemeris, and their verdicts are those of the next section.
- **Time zones (L3).** Before 1970 the engine reads the tzdb 2026f history with `backzone` that it ships (from 2.0.0-rc.3; America/Yellowknife held at tzdata 2025c by the owner's decision), loaded with `prepareLocalTime`, so the 20 vectors tagged `backzone-history` pass; from 1970 it reads the host's `Intl` data. A repeated local time resolves to its earlier instant, and the transition the engine reports gives the offsets of both readings, so the five folds are answered. All 45 pass.
- **TT − UTC and ΔT (L3).** From 1972 to 2027-10-02 the engine takes TAI − UTC from the IERS leap-second list updated 2026-07-06, and UT1 − UTC from IERS: the EOP 20 C04 series in 1972 and `finals2000A.all` of 2026-09-24 from 1973-01-02. The adapter reports TT − UTC as a chart's ΔT (TT − UT1) plus its UT1 − UTC. A leap second itself cannot be expressed as a JavaScript date, so that case is unsupported.
- **Calendars and local mean time (L3).** The 35 calendar vectors are answered by `julianDayNumber` and `dateOfJulianDayNumber`, and the 5 local mean time vectors by `localMeanTimeOffset`, all from `@zodiacs/engine/geo`, with years, months and days in astronomical numbering as the vectors give them. All 40 pass. They are new in 2.0.0-rc.3; earlier releases report these 40 vectors as unsupported.
- **Unsupported (L3).** One vector: the leap second instant above, which a JavaScript date cannot express.
- **Event times (L4).** New in suite 0.3.0. The 70 ingresses are answered by `events()` of `@zodiacs/engine/calc`, its longitude crossing search, on the window each vector gives (TT, or UTC for the 10 tagged `utc-input`); in this run it computes on the DE440 pack. All 70 pass; the largest residual is 1.53 s on TT, and no residual is more than 0.012 of its vector's tolerance. The 2.1.0 prototype adds `searchStations()` and `searchLunations()`. On the shipped pack all 30 stations meet their time tolerance and match direction, and all 40 lunations meet their time tolerance. The largest station residual is +16.155007362365723 s (L4-STA-0030, tolerance 49,110 s). The largest lunation residual is +0.001999590778723359 s (L4-LUN-0028, tolerance 2 s). These results measure the draft build, which still reports package version 2.0.0. The released 2.0.0 archive skips these 70 requests. The signed residuals for both sources and all 70 tolerances are in `docs/evidence/station-lunation-search/residuals.csv`. The design dropped one instant, L4-ING-0060, Pluto's first ingress after 2140-01-01, which falls after the end of the kernel's coverage; it is listed in `vectors/0.3.0/L4-events.json`.

runs.notes:
- **What this run is.** The same adapter and the same build as the section above, started with `--ephemeris astronomy-engine`, which calls `setDefaultEphemeris("astronomy-engine")` first: every request answered on astronomy-engine 2.1.19's series, the engine's fallback outside the DE440 pack's years and what every build before 1.1.0-rc.9 computed on. All 640 vectors are run; outside L1 and L4 its verdicts are the section above's. Up to 2.0.0-rc.2 this file was also the baseline the offline CLI's consumer check held the carried 1.0.0-rc.2 archive to; from 2.0.0-rc.3 that check has its own pinned baseline, `tools/cli/baselines/engine-1.0.0-rc.2-node-22.22.2.json`, the verdicts this file held at `373ceda`.
- **Positions (L1).** 48 pass and 192 fail at 1″. Against DE441 the positions differ by a median of 2.08″ in longitude. The largest differences are 18.8″ in longitude (Neptune) and 19.1″ in latitude (Saturn); the Sun is within 1.64″ and the Moon within 3.75″. These are the verdicts the engine's own section held until 1.1.0-rc.7.
- **Calendars and local mean time (L3).** As in the section above, the 40 calendar and local mean time vectors pass through `julianDayNumber`, `dateOfJulianDayNumber` and `localMeanTimeOffset`, new in 2.0.0-rc.3. The carried 1.0.0-rc.2 archive has none of them and answers those 40 vectors as unsupported, so on them it differs from this file and matches its pinned baseline. The one unsupported vector is the leap second instant.
- **Event times (L4).** The 70 ingresses go through the same `events()` search, here on astronomy-engine's positions: 34 pass and 36 fail, among them one of the 10 in UTC (L4-UTC-0005). The failures follow the positions of L1: a slow body takes long to move the difference, so Neptune's ingress of 2148 (L4-ING-0054) is 10,366 s late, 16 times its tolerance of 649 s. On the prototype all 30 stations pass, including exact direction. The largest time residual is +430.2780179977417 s (L4-STA-0014, tolerance 16,664 s). Of 40 lunations, 21 pass and 19 fail. The largest absolute residual is 10.729984283447266 s early (L4-LUN-0001, tolerance 3 s), and the largest fraction of tolerance is 5.29850435256958 (L4-LUN-0002, tolerance 2 s).

runs.notes:
- **Houses and angles (L2).** Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03 uses the IAU 2006/2000A sidereal time from 1850 to 2050, where its sidereal time agrees with the arbiter's to 0.001″ and its angles and cusps to within 0.007″. Outside that span it switches to its own long-term model. That model's sidereal time is 1.9″ from the IAU value just after 2050, falling to 0.7″ by 2199 (both measured with Swiss's own ΔT); the angles and cusps differ by up to 15.7″ here.
  - All 47 failures are dated after 2050.
  - The vectors before 1850 all pass.
  - Given the arbiter's own sidereal time and obliquity, its house geometry agrees to within 0.0011″ in every system (see `arbiters/l2/README.md`).
- **Flags.** Every position request returned `SEFLG_SWIEPH`: Swiss read its `.se1` files rather than falling back to its Moshier theory.
- **Unsupported.** Swiss Ephemeris has no time zone database and no function for local mean time from a longitude.
